Nginx is a gate that sits between the internet and the servers. When a client requests a resource, the request first goes to this gate. Nginx then determines where the requested resource is located on the server and returns it to the client.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Source: Image by AI & AuthorTraditionally, Nginx was used as a web server, but today it is primarily used as a reverse proxy and handles millions of requests at a time. It acts as the front gate for high-traffic web applications because of its efficient event based architecture.
Let’s first understand the difference between proxy and reverse proxy.
What Is Proxy:
A proxy sits between the client and the internet. It acts on behalf of the client (Here the client is not directly exposed to the server).

• The client sends a request to the proxy.

• The proxy forwards the request to the destination server.

• The server sends the response back to the proxy.

• The proxy returns the response to the client.
In this setup, the proxy represents the client, meaning the destination server only sees the proxy rather than the actual client.
Common uses:

• Hide the client’s IP address

• Access restricted websites

• Content filtering

• Caching frequently accessed content
What Is Reverse Proxy:
A reverse proxy sits between the internet and number of backend servers. It acts on behalf of the servers (Here the server is not exposed directly to the client).

• A client sends a request to the reverse proxy.

• The reverse proxy decides which backend server should handle the request.

• The backend server processes the request.

• The reverse proxy returns the response to the client.
Common uses:

• Load balancing

• SSL/TLS termination

• Caching

• Security (hide backend servers)

• Rate limiting
In this setup, the reverse proxy represents the server, meaning clients interact only with the reverse proxy and never directly with the backend servers.
Note: We need to understand that definitions are based on the system’s perspective. While both feels same they serve totally different purposes.
What Problem Does NGINX Solves:
When a user request hits a server directly, the server creates a thread to process that request. If 1,000 requests arrive simultaneously, the server attempts to create 1,000 threads. Then think about millions… ?
Since the hardware resources such as CPU and RAM are limited, it cannot efficiently spin up such a large number of threads. This leads to excessive memory consumption, increased context switching, and slower response times. As performance degrades, users experience delays or failures, which can result in loosing customers and impact the business.
How NGINX Solves The Problem:
Instead of the client directly hitting the application server, creating a thread for each request. In order to handle millions of concurrent requests, this takes a different approach of running a small number of workers with system calls. This is why it is fast, scalable and helps applications to handle huge traffic.
Working Principle of Nginx:
Nginx spins up and manages worker processes instead of spinning dedicated threads, where each process handles the task via event loop which can handle multiple requests at a time.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Source: Image by AI & AuthorThe initial part is a Master Process. It does not handle requests directly, its job is orchestration and it delegates things to workers. Also there are Worker Processes created based on hardware availability. And these workers juggle among active tasks using an event loop, which is the core part of Nginx. Also, given this, there are a Cache Manager and a Cache Loader which can be used to cache the static resources at startup or a response which is often requested to reduce the unnecessary server loads.
Inside A Worker Process:
The request from the client goes to a queue called the Listen Socket. It establishes a TCP connection, and the connection between the client and Nginx stays open until the client receives the final requested response. This can be anything like HTTP, WebSocket, etc.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Source: Image by AI & AuthorThe Listen Socket queue contains the requests that have not yet started processing by the worker processes. Every request waits here instead of hitting a worker directly.
Once a worker picks up a request and starts processing it, if the request performs any I/O operation, it is then moved to the Connection Socket. The worker immediately switches to another request and continues processing it instead of waiting for entire the I/O operation to complete. Once the I/O is ready, the worker comes back and resumes processing that request.
This concept is called the event loop, where the Nginx worker specializes in juggling multiple requests instead of waiting for a single request to complete. This happens without blocking. In technical terms, this is achieved using system calls (on Linux, this is called as epoll).
If any client is slow, there is a network issue, or the request has a huge payload, it waits in the Listen Socket. Only after the complete request has been received, it make the system call notifying the event loop as there is another new request ready for processing.
Install Nginx On Linux:

• Update package lists:
sudo apt update2. Install Nginx:
sudo apt install nginx -y3. Verify the Installation:
nginx -v4. Start the service:
sudo systemctl start nginx5. Enable it to start on boot as well:
sudo systemctl enable nginx6. Check the Service status:
sudo systemctl status nginxUnderstanding these files makes it much easier for us to configure NGINX.
/etc/nginx/
├── nginx.conf
├── sites-available/
├── sites-enabled/1. nginx.conf (The Main Configuration)
This is the first file NGINX reads when it starts. It sets up global behavior worker processes, connection limits, and, most importantly, which other config files to load.
/etc/nginx/nginx.confuser www-data;
worker_processes auto;events {
worker_connections 768;
}
http {
include /etc/nginx/mime.types;
include /etc/nginx/conf.d/*.conf;
include /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/*;
}
Those include lines tell NGINX to go read other folders for more configuration. Putting every site's config into this one file would get messy fast so instead, nginx.conf acts as the root config, and delegates the actual site definitions elsewhere. That delegation is what the next two folders are for.
2. sites-available/
This directory holds the configuration for every site on the server, active or not.
sites-available/
├── default
├── blog
├── api
├── admin
└── shopsites-available/api:
server {
listen 80;
server_name api.example.com;
root /var/www/api;
}Each file holds one server block for one site. Consider this folder as storage, not the live config a place to keep a site settings even when that site is not running.
Let’s say our server hosts 20 websites and 10 are temporarily paused. We don’t delete their configs we just keep them here, untouched, ready to switch back on later.
3. sites-enabled/
This directory contains only the sites NGINX is currently serving.
sites-enabled/
├── default
├── api
└── blogEntries here are almost always symlinks pointing back to files in sites-available/not copies. NGINX only reads what is in this folder, because nginx.conf includes it
include /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/*;Enabling the API site:
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/api /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/Enabling the blog site:
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/blog /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/NGINX now loads both, because sites-enabled/* picks up every symlink in the folder.
Disabling a site is just as easy remove the symlink, the config stays safe in sites-available/
sudo rm /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/apiThe sites-available / sites-enabled pattern gives us a fast, reversible on/off switch for each site.

• Edit once: Our config lives in exactly one place (sites-available/)

• Toggle instantly: Enabling or disabling a site is just adding or removing a symlink, not editing or duplicating files

• Nothing gets lost: Disabling a site never deletes its configuration
That’s really the whole idea behind NGINX’s configuration structure — keep the global rules in nginx.conf, keep every site's config safely stored in sites-available/, and use sites-enabled/ as the live switchboard deciding what the gate actually lets through. These are the basics and there are even more to explore within Nginx. Because it doesnt act just like a web server, it is a reverse proxy.
